meta.name: CHF Pulmonary Edema — CPAP First-Line, History From the Husband (Practice Summative 913.2)

patient.name: Carol Peters
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe shortness of breath that woke her from sleep about 30 minutes ago and is worsening by the minute; she can speak only one or two words at a time. Per her husband, her chest feels 'very tight and heavy' and her ankles have been swollen for the past couple of days.

history.hpi: 72-year-old female with known congestive heart failure, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation who woke her husband about 30 minutes ago gasping for air. Her dyspnea is severe and progressive — 'it's just getting worse and worse' per the husband. She is too breathless to give her own history and answers only with nods or single words ('Yes,' 'Can't'), so the entire SAMPLE history must come from her husband, Robert. He reports she has had trouble sleeping lying flat for the past two nights, propping herself up with pillows (orthopnea), and that her ankles have been noticeably swollen for the past couple of days. Critically, she takes daily furosemide but he thinks she missed her dose yesterday. He adds, 'This is exactly what happened the last time she had to go to the hospital.' The triad of CHF history, a missed diuretic dose, and worsening orthopnea points squarely at an acute CHF exacerbation with pulmonary edema.
medications: Furosemide 40 mg PO daily ('a water pill' — husband believes she missed her dose yesterday)
Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily (for blood pressure)
Metoprolol tartrate 50 mg PO twice daily
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner around 7 PM last night. Nothing since.
history.events: Trouble sleeping lying flat for the past two nights — she has been propping herself up with pillows. Tonight the breathlessness woke her from a sound sleep about 30 minutes ago and she could not catch her breath. Husband called 911 as it kept getting worse.

scene.dispatch: Medic 2, respond to 456 Oak Avenue, Apartment 3B, for a 72-year-old female with difficulty breathing. Time out is 06:51.
scene.location: Bedroom of a tidy third-floor apartment, accessible by elevator. The patient is sitting upright on the edge of her bed in a nightgown, leaning forward on her outstretched hands. Several pillows are stacked against the headboard where she has been sleeping propped up.
scene.time: Early morning, 06:51 dispatch. Symptoms woke her from sleep roughly 30 minutes ago.
scene.safety: Scene is safe — no immediate hazards. Standard BSI. A worried-looking man in his 70s (the husband) meets the crew at the apartment door.
scene.bystanders: Husband, Robert Peters, is the sole historian — the patient is too dyspneic to speak. He meets the crew at the door: 'Thank goodness you're here! It's my wife, Carol. She woke me up about half an hour ago gasping for air. It's just getting worse and worse.' He stays at her side and answers every SAMPLE question reliably, including the missed furosemide dose and 'this is exactly what happened the last time she had to go to the hospital.'
visualCues: Elderly woman sitting upright on the edge of the bed, leaning forward on outstretched hands — classic tripod position
Anxious expression; breathing rapidly and shallowly with visible accessory muscle use
Can speak only one or two words at a time — nods or says 'Yes' or 'Can't'
Pillows stacked against the headboard — she has been sleeping propped up for two nights
Both ankles and feet visibly swollen (2+ pitting pedal edema on exam)
Worried husband hovering at the bedside, eager to answer questions

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: The crew finds a 72-year-old woman tripoding on the edge of her bed in obvious, severe respiratory distress: RR 34 and labored, SpO2 86% on room air, one-to-two-word dyspnea, accessory muscle use, and skin that is pale, cool, and diaphoretic. Auscultation reveals coarse crackles (rales) throughout all lung fields, most prominent at the bases, with NO wheeze. Both ankles show 2+ pitting edema. Her radial pulse is rapid and irregularly irregular — her known A-Fib — at 118, with a BP of 188/102. She is alert and oriented but physically cannot give a history — the whole story lives with her husband: CHF, hypertension, A-Fib, a missed furosemide dose yesterday, and two nights of worsening orthopnea. This is the assessment fork the scenario is built on. MATC's Respiratory Distress guideline distinguishes bronchospastic etiology (wheezing, asthma/COPD history) from fluid-overload etiology (rales, peripheral edema, CHF and diuretic history) — and every finding on this patient lands in the fluid-overload column. That pattern routes her to CPAP, NOT to a nebulizer, and NOT to a non-rebreather alone. A non-rebreather raises FiO2 but does nothing about the fluid-filled alveoli; positive pressure is the mechanical fix, and the protocol says NIV should be administered for severe respiratory distress. A teaching point rides along: the missed 'water pill' explains the mechanism, but replacing it is not field therapy — the protocol notes pulmonary edema is more commonly a volume-distribution problem, and diuretics like furosemide provide no immediate benefit and can cause significant harm. For this crew the treatment IS positioning, oxygen, and CPAP, with early transport and hospital notification carrying the rest. The clock starts now — she is working hard, and patients this age do not sustain a respiratory rate of 34 for long.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent. No foreign body obstruction. Speaking single words only due to respiratory effort
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 34, rapid, shallow, and labored with visible accessory muscle use; coarse crackles (rales) throughout all lung fields, most prominent at the bases; NO wheezing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, rapid, and irregularly irregular; skin pale, cool, and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities; too fatigued and dyspneic to ambulate
otherFindings: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time — answers with nods or single words ('Yes,' 'Can't')
Coarse crackles in ALL fields, worst at the bases — with pedal edema and CHF history this is the fluid-overload pattern, NOT bronchospasm
2+ pitting pedal edema in both ankles and feet
Irregularly irregular radial pulse — consistent with her known A-Fib
History must come from the husband — she cannot speak in sentences
Missed furosemide dose yesterday + two nights of orthopnea = the mechanism
BGL 130 mg/dL by glucometer
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (one or two words at a time, nodding) Can't… breathe. …Yes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rapid primary survey — recognize severe respiratory distress (hypoxia, retractions, 1–2 word speech)
expectedActions.rationale: She shows nearly every distress sign the protocol lists: anxiety, SpO2 86% (below the 90% hypoxia threshold), accessory muscle use, and inability to speak full sentences. Naming the severity out loud is what justifies going straight to CPAP instead of titrating up slowly from a cannula.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Signs of distress include: Apprehension, anxiety, combativeness. Hypoxia (less than 90% oxygen saturation). Intercostal/subcostal/supraclavicular retractions, accessory muscle use. Grunting, stridor, inability to speak full sentences. Nasal flaring. Cyanosis.

expectedActions.shortAction: Full set of vitals — pulse, BP, RR, neuro status, temperature, SpO2 (BGL 130 by glucometer)
expectedActions.rationale: The numbers anchor everything that follows: SpO2 86% is the hypoxia that mandates escalation, BP 188/102 documents the hypertensive strain, and the irregularly irregular pulse at 118 matches her known A-Fib. The baseline set is also what every post-intervention reassessment is measured against.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Exam: Full set of vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment), temperature, and O2 saturation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Identify fluid-overload pattern (rales, pedal edema, CHF/diuretic history) — NOT bronchospasm
expectedActions.rationale: This differentiation is the entire scenario. Rales in all fields, 2+ pedal edema, CHF history, diuretic therapy, and hypertension check every box in the protocol's fluid-overload column; there is no wheeze and no asthma/COPD history. The pattern selects the pulmonary edema pathway — positive pressure with CPAP — over bronchodilators.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Etiology of respiratory distress: Bronchospastic etiology (e.g., asthma, COPD) is suggested by: Wheezing on auscultation; "Shark fin" waveform capnograph or prolonged expiratory phase; History of asthma/COPD. Fluid overload etiology (e.g., CHF, pulmonary edema) is suggested by: Jugular venous distention; Rales on auscultation; Peripheral edema; History of CHF, diuretic therapy, dialysis noncompliance, hypertension.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain SAMPLE from the husband — onset, prior episodes, missed furosemide, hospitalizations
expectedActions.rationale: Her dyspnea prevents her from giving her own history — the husband is the only historian. The protocol's history elements (onset, treatments prior to EMS, hospitalization history) all come from him, and the missed furosemide dose plus 'this is exactly what happened last time' confirms the working diagnosis.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: History: Onset of symptoms. Treatments prior to EMS: Oxygen, inhaler, nebulizer, other treatments, chronic or recent steroids. Hospitalizations: Number of emergency department visits in the past year, number of hospital admissions in the past year, number of ICU admissions (ever), previously intubated (ever).

expectedActions.shortAction: High-flow O2 immediately, then escalate to CPAP — target SpO2 94–98%
expectedActions.rationale: At SpO2 86% with severe distress, the protocol's escalation ladder does not stop at a non-rebreather: NIV should be administered for severe respiratory distress. Oxygen buys minutes; positive pressure treats the problem. The crew that stalls on an NRB alone is on the deterioration branch of this scenario.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be administered for severe respiratory distress via BVM, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP).

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep her upright in position of comfort — do not lay her flat
expectedActions.rationale: She has self-selected the position that keeps her alveoli driest — two nights of pillows and now a tripod. The protocol notes positioning significantly impacts respiratory mechanics and that elevating the head improves the ability to ventilate; forcing her supine for packaging would worsen the edema and her work of breathing.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient positioning can significantly impact respiratory mechanics. Elevating the head or padding (shoulders, occiput) can assist with opening airway and respiratory mechanics. This can both improve the ability to ventilate and limit aspiration.

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, explains the procedure in a calm reassuring voice, correctly assembles the CPAP device on high-flow oxygen, applies the mask with a good seal, and coaches the patient through the initial anxiety of positive pressure.

Crew fails to recognize the need for CPAP, significantly delays its application, or applies only a non-rebreather mask. The NRB raises FiO2 but does nothing for the flooded alveoli; over roughly 10 minutes the patient fatigues, hypoxia worsens, and she slides into decompensated respiratory failure.

phases.name: CPAP applied
phases.description: The crew explains the mask to Mrs. Peters in a calm, confident voice — 'this is going to feel like sticking your head out a car window, but it will make breathing easier; breathe with it, not against it' — and holds it to her face before strapping it, letting her acclimate. CPAP starts at 5 cm H2O on high-flow oxygen and is stepped up 2–3 cm H2O at a time as tolerated, per the MATC PEEP titration ladder (goal: the lowest pressure that does the job; physician consultation for anything over 10–15). Her first instinct is to claw at the mask — that anxiety is presumed to be hypoxia and air hunger, and per protocol it is treated with ventilatory support and reassurance; there is no shortcut around a calm voice and a steady hand. Within a couple of minutes of a good seal her SpO2 begins to climb and the respiratory rate starts down. The discipline now is twofold: keep the seal — breaking the circuit dumps the airway pressure the crew just spent minutes building — and keep the reassessment cycle running, with RR, SpO2, work of breathing, breath sounds, mental status, and a fresh set of vitals after each titration step while the second provider readies the stretcher for an upright, mask-on transport.
phases.triggerCondition: CPAP assembled correctly, connected to high-flow oxygen, applied with a good mask seal, and the patient coached through the initial anxiety. PEEP titrated stepwise from 5 cm H2O.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent under the CPAP mask; good seal achieved after coaching
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR trending down through the high 20s; accessory muscle use beginning to ease; crackles still audible in all fields but no longer worsening
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse rapid and irregularly irregular, slightly slower; skin still pale and cool but diaphoresis no longer worsening
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities; initially reaches for the mask, settles with coaching
otherFindings: First 60 seconds on the mask are the hardest — she needs continuous verbal coaching to tolerate it
Anxiety on NIV is presumed due to hypoxia — treat with ventilatory support and reassurance
CPAP at 5 cm H2O initial, stepped up 2–3 cm H2O as tolerated to lowest effective pressure
SBP 176 — recheck a full set of vitals after each titration step and at least every 5 minutes
SpO2 climbing; do NOT break the mask seal to auscultate or reposition
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (muffled through the mask, eyes wide, then settling) …okay. …okay.

expectedActions.shortAction: Explain the mask, reassure, and coach her through the first minutes of CPAP
expectedActions.rationale: The protocol is explicit that coaching IS the intervention that makes NIV work in a mask-naive patient. A technically perfect CPAP setup fails if the patient rips it off; a calm, confident provider is what carries her through the initial smothering sensation.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The key to successful use of NIV in a patient who has not used it before is coaching and explanation of the process and reassurance of the patient.

expectedActions.shortAction: CPAP with PEEP 5 cm H2O initial; increase 2–3 cm H2O stepwise to lowest effective level
expectedActions.rationale: MATC does not name a fixed CPAP number — it gives a titration ladder: start at 5 cm H2O, step up 2–3 at a time while letting her equilibrate, and seek the lowest pressure that meets the goals, because higher PEEP carries greater hemodynamic cost. Physician consultation is the gate for pressures beyond 10–15.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: PEEP — 5 cmH2O is generally an appropriate initial PEEP setting. Increase PEEP in stepwise fashion (2–3 cmH2O at a time) as necessary, allowing time for the patient to equilibrate with each change before further adjustments are made. The goal is to reach the lowest PEEP needed to adequately ventilate the patient. Higher PEEP results in greater negative hemodynamic impact. Generally, physician consultation should be considered for higher PEEP levels (greater than 10–15 cmH2O).

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess RR, SpO2, work of breathing, breath sounds, and mental status after each intervention
expectedActions.rationale: The protocol requires the exam be documented at baseline and after EACH intervention — every PEEP step and every few minutes on the mask gets a fresh look. The serial record is what proves the intervention is working and what catches deterioration early enough to act on it.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Document key aspects of the exam at baseline and after each intervention: Respiratory rate. Oxygen saturation. Use of accessory muscles. Breath sounds and quality. Mental status. Response to interventions.

transitions.condition: Patient tolerates the mask with continuous coaching, PEEP is titrated stepwise to effect, and the crew reassesses after each change. Approximately 5–10 minutes after application, work of breathing visibly decreases, oxygenation climbs, and she comes out of the tripod position.

Crew breaks the circuit or removes the mask prematurely (to auscultate, to move her, or because her anxiety was mismanaged) and falls back to a non-rebreather. The airway pressure collapses, atelectasis recurs, and she decompensates abruptly — the same respiratory-failure endpoint as never applying CPAP at all.

phases.name: Improving on CPAP
phases.description: Five to ten minutes after application, the intervention is visibly working. Mrs. Peters is calmer, her work of breathing has significantly decreased, and she is no longer tripoding — she is sitting back against the raised head of the stretcher. She can speak in full sentences through the mask: 'Oh, thank you. That is so much better. I can finally catch my breath.' Vitals confirm what the eyes see: BP down to 164/92 as the positive pressure and easing work of breathing take the catecholamine strain off, heart rate 104 and still irregularly irregular, RR 22 and unlabored, SpO2 96% on CPAP. Skin is pink, warm, and less diaphoretic. The crew's job now is to not undo it: keep the mask sealed and the circuit intact — breaking the seal dumps airway pressure and invites abrupt decompensation via atelectasis — keep reassessing against the NIV goals of care (air hunger down, SpO2 at or above 94%, RR normalizing), and keep the serial vitals coming every 5 minutes. She still needs definitive care; improvement on CPAP is a reason to move, not a reason to stay and admire the numbers. Package her sitting up with CPAP in place and let the receiving hospital know what is coming.
phases.triggerCondition: Approximately 5–10 minutes of continuous CPAP with the seal maintained and PEEP titrated to effect: work of breathing significantly decreased, tripod position resolved, speaking in full sentences, SpO2 96% on the mask, BP trending down.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent under CPAP; seal maintained continuously
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 22 and unlabored; accessory muscle use resolved; crackles receding toward the bases
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse 104, irregularly irregular, good quality; skin perfusion visibly improved
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities; relaxed on the stretcher, no longer bracing
otherFindings: Visibly less anxious; out of the tripod position
Speaking in FULL sentences through the mask — a direct marker of decreased work of breathing
BP 164/92 and trending down as work of breathing eases — continue serial vitals every 5 minutes
NIV goals of care being met: decreased air hunger, SpO2 ≥ 94%, RR normalizing
Do NOT break the mask seal — not for auscultation, not for movement, not for conversation
She still requires definitive care at the hospital — package sitting up with CPAP in place
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (through the mask, full sentences) Oh, thank you. That is so much better. I can finally catch my breath.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain a continuous mask seal — never break the circuit once she is tolerating it
expectedActions.rationale: Every centimeter of airway pressure recruited over the last ten minutes lives behind that seal. The protocol warns that breaking the circuit causes significant atelectasis that takes time to reverse — the gains are not stored, they are maintained.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For any patient on NIV, focus on maintaining a continuous mask seal is essential to maximizing the positive impact of PEEP, particularly at higher levels. Breaking the circuit or removing the mask should be meticulously avoided, as the significant atelectasis will occur which will take time to reverse.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess against NIV goals: air hunger down, SpO2 ≥ 94%, RR normalizing
expectedActions.rationale: The protocol defines what 'working' means for NIV so the crew is not guessing: decreased air hunger, SpO2 at or above 94%, respiratory rate normalizing. She is meeting all three. It also cautions that more support than needed is not better — the titration goal is enough, not maximum.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: NIV goals of therapy will vary based on patient presentation and history. More support than is needed to relieve symptoms or "normal" is not necessarily better in these patients. Goals of care may include: Decreased air hunger. SPO2 of ≥ 94%. Normalization of respiratory rate (decreased tachypnea).

expectedActions.shortAction: Document the serial exam — RR, SpO2, breath sounds, mental status, response to each intervention
expectedActions.rationale: The before-and-after picture — RR 34 to 22, SpO2 86% to 96%, tripod to full sentences — is both the clinical proof the pathway worked and the documentation the protocol names element by element.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Document key aspects of the exam at baseline and after each intervention: Respiratory rate. Oxygen saturation. Use of accessory muscles. Breath sounds and quality. Mental status. Response to interventions.

transitions.condition: Patient packaged sitting upright with CPAP in place and the circuit never broken; transport initiated to the closest appropriate facility with reassessment every 5 minutes en route and early notification to the receiving hospital so their CPAP can be staged for the switchover.

phases.name: Transported on CPAP
phases.description: Mrs. Peters is transported sitting upright with CPAP in place, the circuit intact, and a fresh set of vitals every 5 minutes. She remains improved: RR 20, SpO2 97%, BP drifting down through the 150s. The two rules that govern this phase are both about the mask. First: the mask does NOT come off until she is on the emergency department stretcher with hospital CPAP immediately ready for the switchover (or a physician at the bedside directs otherwise) — the protocol is emphatic that breaking the seal drops airway pressure and can cause abrupt decompensation through atelectasis and alveolar collapse, and 'we're here' is not an indication to remove it. Second: the crew watches for deterioration ON the mask — worsening mental status, vomiting, climbing respiratory rate or falling saturation — because the protocol's answer to failing NIV is to remove it and escalate airway management (for this crew, BVM with adjuncts), not to hope. Early radio notification gives the emergency department time to have their own CPAP assembled at the bedside. Handoff includes the full arc: initial presentation, vitals trend, CPAP settings and titration steps, and the husband's history including the missed furosemide dose.
phases.triggerCondition: Transport initiated with CPAP in place and seal maintained; 5-minute reassessments continuing en route; patient stable and improved.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent under CPAP; seal continuous since application
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 20, easy; crackles now limited to the bases
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 98, irregularly irregular; warm and dry
otherFindings: CPAP stays on until the ED stretcher with hospital CPAP immediately available — arrival is not an indication for removal
Watching for deterioration on NIV: worsening mental status or vomiting → remove CPAP and escalate to BVM with adjuncts
Serial vitals every 5 minutes en route; early radio notification lets the ED stage their CPAP for switchover
Handoff: presentation, vitals trend, CPAP titration steps, missed furosemide dose, husband's history
Initial hypoxia (86%) corrected to target range by arrival — the performance measure the protocol tracks
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (through the mask) I feel so much better than I did. Is my husband following us?

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep CPAP on until she is on the ED stretcher with hospital CPAP immediately ready
expectedActions.rationale: The most common place this therapy is undone is the ED doorway. The protocol's directive is unambiguous: the mask does not come off until the hospital circuit is immediately available for switchover or a physician at the bedside says so — because breaking the seal can cause abrupt decompensation after everything the crew just fixed.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Once initiated and patient is tolerating mask, DO NOT discontinue CPAP/BiPAP until patient is on the emergency department stretcher and hospital CPAP/BiPAP is immediately available for patient to be switched over, or physician is at bedside and requesting CPAP/BiPAP be discontinued. Breaking the mask seal causes a significant decrease in airway pressures and may lead to abrupt decompensation due to atelectasis and alveolar collapse.

expectedActions.shortAction: Watch for deterioration on CPAP (worse mentation, vomiting) — remove and escalate if it appears
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous reassessment en route is not ceremonial — the protocol defines the failure signs that mandate a change of plan. If her mental status worsens or she vomits into the mask, CPAP comes off and airway management escalates to BVM with adjuncts.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If patient deteriorates on CPAP/BiPAP (e.g., worsened mental status, increasing EtCO2, vomiting), remove CPAP/BiPAP and escalate airway management options as above.

expectedActions.shortAction: Bedside handoff with vitals trend, CPAP titration steps, and the missed-furosemide history
expectedActions.rationale: The receiving team inherits a patient who looks far better than she did 20 minutes ago; the documented baseline exam and per-intervention responses are what convey how sick she actually was and what is holding her together.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Document key aspects of the exam at baseline and after each intervention: Respiratory rate. Oxygen saturation. Use of accessory muscles. Breath sounds and quality. Mental status. Response to interventions.

phases.name: CPAP delayed; NRB only
phases.description: The crew either never recognized the CPAP indication, delayed it too long, settled for a non-rebreather, or broke the seal after starting — and about ten minutes into the call, fatigue wins. The non-rebreather raised her FiO2, but oxygen cannot cross alveoli that are full of fluid; the mechanical problem was never addressed. Her respiratory effort weakens as she exhausts, breathing slows to 10 shallow breaths a minute bordering on agonal, and her level of consciousness falls — she now responds to verbal stimuli only with a moan, slumping back on the bed, no longer able to hold the tripod position that was keeping her alive. SpO2 is 75% ON the non-rebreather, BP has climbed to 205/112, and the heart rate is 130 and thready. This is decompensated respiratory failure progressing to respiratory arrest, and the window for CPAP has closed: NIV needs a patient who is awake, can follow commands, and can maintain her own airway — she can do none of the three. The MATC Airway Management pathway now governs: two-person BVM with PEEP supporting her spontaneous respirations at 10–12 breaths per minute, head elevated up to 30 degrees, an NPA while her gag is intact, suction staged at the head, an SGA if BVM with adjuncts cannot maintain oxygenation, and rapid transport for airway stabilization — requesting an ALS intercept en route if one is available, though ventilation cannot wait for it. Restoring oxygenation and ventilation is the whole job; there is no medication fix on this truck, and there was never one that mattered more than positive pressure.
phases.triggerCondition: CPAP was never applied, was significantly delayed, was replaced by a non-rebreather alone, or the seal was broken after initiation. Roughly 10 minutes from initial contact, the patient exhausts: respiratory effort weakens, breathing slows to 10/min and shallow, and she becomes responsive to verbal stimuli only with a moan — decompensated respiratory failure progressing toward respiratory arrest.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but threatened — she can no longer reliably protect it; gag reflex still present; suction ready
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 10, shallow, bordering on agonal; minimal chest rise; respiratory effort visibly weakening; crackles now with scattered gurgling
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse 130, thready, irregularly irregular; skin pale, cool, diaphoretic with dusky lips
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Slumped back on the bed; withdraws weakly; no longer able to maintain tripod position
otherFindings: SpO2 75% ON the non-rebreather — FiO2 was never the problem; the flooded alveoli were
Responds to verbal stimuli with a moan only — the CPAP window (awake, obeys commands, protects airway) has closed
RR 10 and shallow with minimal chest rise — hypoventilation, respiratory failure
BP 205/112 and HR 130 thready — decompensating under catecholamine strain
Losing the tripod position is a pre-arrest sign, not relaxation
RESCUE ORDER: two-person BVM + PEEP supporting her spontaneous breaths → NPA → SGA if BVM fails → rapid transport
Request ALS intercept if available — but ventilation cannot wait for it
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (moans to verbal stimuli only — no words)

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize respiratory failure — two-person BVM with PEEP now, head elevated up to 30°
expectedActions.rationale: She is in respiratory failure, and BVM ventilation is the protocol's answer — two-person, two-thumbs-up technique, PEEP attached (positive pressure is still the therapy her alveoli need), and the head of the bed up. This is the same physiologic treatment CPAP would have delivered, now applied by hand because the window for a cooperative NIV patient closed.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest. Whenever possible, the patient's head should be elevated up to 30 degrees. Two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation is preferred. PEEP should be used with BVM: 5 cmH2O is generally an appropriate initial PEEP setting.

expectedActions.shortAction: Support her spontaneous breaths; ventilate 10–12/min with just enough volume for chest rise
expectedActions.rationale: She is hypoventilating, not apneic — the protocol says support spontaneous respirations, at the adult rate of 10–12 with tidal volumes of roughly 6–8 mL/kg (about 400–540 mL for her 68 kg). Overventilation drops preload and cardiac output in a patient whose hemodynamics are already strained; the goal is enough, timed with her own efforts.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Support spontaneous respirations if the patient is hypoventilating. Rate: Adult: 10–12 breaths/minute. Tidal volume: Ventilate with just enough volume to see chest rise, approximately 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight. Over-inflation (e.g., excessive tidal volume) and overventilation (e.g., excessive minute ventilation) are both undesirable and potentially harmful.

expectedActions.shortAction: Place an NPA (gag intact); OPA only if gag is lost; suction staged
expectedActions.rationale: An adjunct makes the BVM seal and ventilation more effective. She still moans to voice and retains a gag, which selects the NPA; if she deteriorates further and the gag disappears, the OPA replaces it. Suction stays within reach — a fluid-flooded airway can soil quickly.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Oropharyngeal airways (OPA) or nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be placed if needed to maintain a patent airway and make BVM ventilation more effective: OPA are used for patients without gag reflex. NPA are used for patients with gag reflex. Suction airway: for significantly contaminated airways, consider utilizing a suction assisted laryngeal airway decontamination (SALAD) technique.

expectedActions.shortAction: If BVM with adjuncts cannot oxygenate — place an appropriately sized SGA
expectedActions.rationale: The escalation ladder is explicit: BVM with OPA/NPA first, then a supraglottic airway if that is not maintaining oxygenation and ventilation. The least invasive effective airway wins, and the SGA is the ceiling of this crew's ladder.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Supraglottic airways (SGA): Consider the use of an appropriately sized SGA if BVM (with OPA/NPA) alone is not effective in maintaining oxygenation and/or ventilation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rapid transport to the closest appropriate hospital for airway stabilization
expectedActions.rationale: A patient in respiratory failure that field interventions are barely holding belongs at the closest appropriate hospital, per the protocol's own transport directive. The debrief writes itself from the timestamps: the ten minutes spent on a non-rebreather were the ten minutes that put her here.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport to the closest appropriate hospital for airway stabilization when respiratory failure cannot be successfully managed in the prehospital setting.
